title: New US missile appears to have killed Iranian civilians far from its blast site, expert report says
description: It has been touted by the manufacturer as the ballistic missile of the future: lethal, long-range, and pinpoint.  Lockheed Martin’s Precision Strike Missile has the U.S. military investing billions to...
fullText:
It has been touted by the manufacturer as the ballistic missile of the future: lethal, long-range, and pinpoint. Lockheed Martin's Precision Strike Missile has the U.S. military investing billions to update its arsenal.

But a close look at what is believed to be its first use in combat — on the first day of the Iran war — highlights the potential peril of deploying this weapon near population centers because it appears to spray pellets over a wide area, according to a review by the conflict monitor Airwars and interviews with weapons experts and former defense officials.

Three missiles that struck the southern city of Lamerd on Feb. 28 killed civilians as far as 50 meters (164 feet) from where they detonated, and caused damage more than three times farther away, Airwars found. The missiles detonated above a sports complex and two residential neighborhoods, Airwars found. The blasts killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to Iranian officials.

Airwars is the first to map the damage radius of the strikes in Lamerd and estimate the lethal range of the weapon used.

The PrSM is designed to explode midair and propel tens of thousands of dense metal pellets at high speed in all directions. Photos, videos and satellite images of the Lamerd strikes' aftermath analyzed by Airwars and verified by The Associated Press show buildings, streets and vehicles were heavily pockmarked in a blast pattern that experts say is consistent with the PrSM's capabilities.

The U.S. military has confirmed firing PrSMs into Iran, but has denied attacking Lamerd.

It is unclear who or what was the intended target in Lamerd. An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps compound is located nearby, but satellite images showed no damage there.

Six weapons experts, including two who are former military officials, told AP they believe PrSMs struck Lamerd — and they said it was unlikely that Israeli or Iranian weapons were used. All said militaries should avoid firing the PrSM at targets near civilian areas.

"You would be hard-pressed to find a reason to use the PrSM in a densely populated area," said Michael Meier, a former U.S. Army adviser on the laws of war.

Airwars, a London-based nonprofit, was founded more than a decade ago to track reports of civilian deaths from U.S. airstrikes in Syria and Iraq, and it has also monitored conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine and elsewhere. It relies on publicly available material, such as photos, videos, satellite images, social media and news reports, and uses geolocation software and other tools to help it analyze this evidence.

Airwars used these methods to investigate the strikes on Lamerd. It mapped the approximate locations of the missiles' detonations, where civilians were reported killed and where damage was visible and consistent with blast patterns. It then measured the distances between the positions to estimate the blast radius.

AP verified Airwars' blast radius estimate by measuring the distance between where civilians were killed, based on Iranian media reports, and where the missiles detonated midair, based on security camera and other videos. AP also examined satellite images, photos and videos of damage from the attack sites.

Lockheed Martin, which did not respond to a request for comment, has not said how wide the missile's impact is. It has released an animated video modeling a PrSM blast.

In a post to X on March 1, the day after Lamerd was struck, U.S. Central Command included what munitions experts say was an image of the PrSM being fired during the Iran operation. Three days later, it touted that PrSMs — in a "historic first" — had been used in Iran, though not where.

Several weeks later, as reports about the strikes in Lamerd garnered media attention, a spokesperson for Central Command said in a statement that U.S. forces did not launch PrSMs or any weapons into Lamerd on Feb. 28, and that they do not target civilians. The spokesperson said footage of one of the strikes suggested it was an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.

Weapons experts said a missile seen in security camera video from Lamerd does not match that Iranian model, which has a rounded engine.

The Israeli military told AP it did not strike anywhere in Iran as far south as Lamerd on the first day of the war, and experts said Israel's military is not known to have missiles that detonate midair.

When asked about Airwars' and AP's findings, U.S. Central Command reiterated its denial of responsibility, saying that was based on an earlier review of what happened there. Its commander, Adm. Brad Cooper, also told Congress in May that they were only investigating one case of U.S. fire killing civilians — a strike on an Iranian school in Minab.

The new missiles are meant to replace the Army Tactical Missile System used for decades, according to the U.S. military.

While the ATACMS can travel approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles), the PrSM can hit targets over 499 kilometers (310 miles) away, Lockheed Martin says.

The PrSM differs from its predecessor in another key way. Where ATACMS shatter into steel fragments or small bomblets over their target area, an exploding PrSM fires tens of thousands of pellets made of tungsten in all directions, Airwars and weapons experts say.

Because of tungsten's high density and melting point, the pellets retain their shape after detonation. That makes them extremely lethal, capable of piercing soft armor, according to defense journals.

Airwars found footage of a school in Lamerd that was damaged by the missile detonated over the Shahid Naimi Sports Hall about 170 meters (557 feet) away.

That blast killed seven civilians, mostly children, Iranian state media reported. Airwars says it used open-source material to confirm the deaths. Among them were three teenage girls playing volleyball and a woman smoking a hookah in front of her house.

A separate blast over the Tal-e Khandagh neighborhood killed 2-year-old Avina Barzegar, who was playing in her yard. Airwars estimates the pellet that struck Barzegar traveled 50 meters from the blast site. It reached that conclusion by geolocating her house, based on a video showing its front gate, and measuring the distance from the house to the site.

Neither Airwars nor AP could find any reports indicating that military or security personnel were killed in the strikes, or that military infrastructure was hit.

Since the Lamerd strikes, the Pentagon signed a contract worth over $4 billion with Lockheed Martin to quadruple PrSM production. The U.K. said in June it had set aside 130 million pounds ($177 million) to procure the weapon. Australia bought the missiles in 2025 and in April invested billions of dollars into the PrSM program.

Weapons experts say the PrSM provides valuable new capabilities, but it should be used carefully.

"Its proper use should be reserved for things like large concentrations of enemy personnel with hard and soft armor," said Wes Bryant, a former Pentagon adviser on precision warfare and civilian harm mitigation.

Trevor Ball, a former explosives expert for the U.S. Army, also urged caution.

"It will kill people outside their homes who aren't protected by walls," he said.

title: Analysis-Toyota and Honda may get stuck with the bill for Trump’s Canada tariffs
description: President Donald Trump is targeting Ottawa with a proposed 50% tariff on Canadian car imports — but Japan's Toyota and Honda may end up footing the bill. The two Japanese automakers account for more than three-quarters of all ‌cars made in Canada.
fullText:
TOKYO, Aug 31 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump is targeting Ottawa with a proposed 50% tariff on Canadian car imports — but Japan's Toyota and Honda may end up footing the bill.

The two Japanese automakers account for more than three-quarters of all ‌cars made in Canada. They could be forced to shutter some production lines if the tariffs go into effect on January 1 as proposed, ‌analysts said.

How are automakers adapting to changing trade policies?

What percentage of Toyota and Honda production comes from Canada?

How would Trump's proposed tariffs impact Japanese automakers?

What are the broader implications for Canada's auto industry?

While a deal could still be reached, the timing of the U.S. tariffs couldn't be worse, as Japanese automakers are being stung by competition from low-cost Chinese EVs in markets such as Southeast Asia, ​Europe and Latin America.

The United States remains Toyota and Honda's biggest market and, crucially, one where Chinese rivals like BYD aren't allowed in.

Canadian-built cars accounted for almost a quarter of Honda's U.S. sales and 17% of Toyota's last year, the most among major automakers, according to Barclays analysts. As a result, the two face the biggest potential hit from Trump's plan to double the levies from the current 25%.

"If you really wanted to destroy the Canadian auto industry, you could with these tariffs," said Julie Boote, ‌autos analyst at Pelham Smithers Associates in London.

Both companies ⁠would likely have to close some of their Canadian assembly lines, she said.

Toyota and Honda declined to comment.

Canada's auto industry produces around 1.2 million cars a year and indirectly supports some 427,000 jobs. Toyota's exports from Canada to the United States ⁠include the RAV4, while Honda exports the CR-V. Both cars are among the best-selling SUVs in the United States.

The proposed tariffs are the latest example of Trump trade policies that have left the global auto industry scrambling to adapt. For years, U.S., European, Japanese and South Korean car companies and their suppliers built production chains across North America, taking advantage ​of ​cross-border trade deals and, especially in Mexico, lower labour costs.

But cost dynamics have now changed ​drastically. U.S. tariffs cost Toyota some 1.4 trillion yen ($8.8 billion) in ‌the last financial year.

Toyota is now doubling down on U.S. production. The world's largest automaker last year said it aims to invest up to $10 billion over five years to expand its U.S. operations. That will include a new $3.6 billion auto plant in Texas, where it intends to move production of the Tacoma pick-up truck from its Baja California plant in Mexico.

For Honda, which is struggling to turn around its money-losing car business, tariffs have only added to the strain.

title: Ukrainians slapped twin AK rifles on a drone with wheels to make a cheap mobile turret
description: Kyiv has been looking to cheaper assault drones that it can scale rapidly to reduce the risks to its infantry.
fullText:
Ukraine has built a drone turret using two Kalashnikov rifles as its main attack option.

They're a cheap platform that the country's defense tech incubator, Brave1, says it can scale quickly.

It's already been used in combat, with more than 5 units testing it operationally, Brave1 said.

A Ukrainian manufacturer developed a roving turret with two Kalashnikov assault rifles for its main armament, as Kyiv aims to build more cheap ground drones to fill dangerous infantry roles.

The uncrewed ground vehicle was recently used in combat by the Security Service of Ukraine's Alpha Group special forces to destroy a Russian ambush drone, said the country's defense tech incubator, Brave1, on Thursday.

"Why the Kalashnikov? The reason is simple: It's the most widely available small arm across our military units," the incubator wrote in a social media post, adding that using the assault rifle allowed its forces to "rapidly scale" the drones on the front lines.

Neither the drone nor the manufacturer was named, though Brave1 said the drone's creator is a member of its platform. The Kalashnikov design was built for a technical brief issued by Brave1.

A Ukrainian robot destroys a Russian ambush drone with dual-wielded Kalashnikov rifles — this is the reality on the frontline in Ukraine.

A Brave1 member company developed a specialized turret for the Kalashnikov based on our technical brief. It took them less than 6 months to… pic.twitter.com/ocd962Kium

— BRAVE1 (@BRAVE1ua) August 27, 2026

More than five Ukrainian units are operationally testing the drone, Brave1 added.

Footage of the turret shows the two Kalashnikov rifles mounted closely to each other on a frame attached to a pan-and-tilt gimbal, which in turn rests on a four-wheeled platform.

Each rifle appears to be modified behind the grip and trigger guard to remotely receive fire commands, though no other significant tweaks are visible.

Notably, Brave1 showed clips of a person manually reloading one of the Kalashnikovs with a box magazine and then racking the bolt, indicating that the turret's current design still requires a soldier nearby to help it stay in a prolonged fight.

Ukraine has been developing uncrewed ground vehicles for all manner of tasks, including ground assault, artillery cover, casualty evacuation, mine-clearing, and logistics for years.

They've been a major, though not complete, solution for its shortage of soldiers on the front lines and forward areas, which have become saturated with drones and deadly to cross or navigate.

The new Kalashnikov turret points to a Ukrainian emphasis on building cheaper, simpler systems to be built quickly for the war.

"We are scaling cheap combat UGVs and robotizing the front line to reduce risks to our infantry," Brave1 said in its post.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Chicago mayor demands companies reveal whether leaders ‘reflect diversity’ for city contracts
description: DHS accused Brandon Johnson of punishing businesses that help ICE enforce federal immigration law after the Chicago mayor signed a new executive order.
fullText:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order on Wednesday requiring city contractors to disclose information about leadership diversity demographics, as well as report whether they have any ties to certain law enforcement agencies such as ICE, as he moves to use the city's purchasing power to impose new contracting standards.

Johnson said workplace data was necessary to identify discrimination and criticized the Trump administration's efforts to end federal reporting requirements.

"If you want to do business with this city, we want to know whether the people leading your company reflect the diversity of the communities whose tax dollars are paying your contracts," Johnson said.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Johnson of punishing American companies for assisting federal immigration enforcement.

Democrat Mayor Blasted By Dhs For 'Hunting Down' Property Owners Leasing To Ice: 'Unhinged'

"If Mayor Johnson wants to lecture anyone about taxpayer dollars, remember what he is: a sanctuary politician who bullies American companies with money that isn't his. Chicago takes the federal check, but it won't enforce the federal law," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday.

"In case Chicago's mayor forgot, an oath of office is a commitment to upholding the law, not encouraging criminal illegal aliens to break it," they added.

"Make no mistake, we will not be deterred. Under President Trump, ICE will keep enforcing the law in Chicago, whether City Hall likes it or not," the spokesperson said.

The Chicago mayor unveiled the order during a press conference at Arise Chicago, a nonprofit that works to protect immigrants' rights. Johnson framed the order as a response to corporate influence in Washington and said Chicago would use city spending to put its values into practice.

The order also directs Chicago's chief procurement officer to develop rules within 90 days barring vendors found to have committed public integrity, workplace discrimination or wage theft violations during the previous five years.

Contractors must disclose whether they received more than $500,000 from government or law enforcement agencies or face proceedings alleging excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing, discrimination or other civil rights violations.

Trump Admin Wants To Stop Illinois City's Reparations Effort For 'Simply Handing Out Money Based On Race'

Large private companies with corporate families reporting at least $1 billion in net income must provide information about leadership diversity, board composition and diversity policies when not already covered by Illinois reporting law.

Under the order, contractors must also report efforts to hire and promote formerly incarcerated people, and future awardees must update the disclosures at least annually.

Doing business with ICE alone is not listed as a disqualifying offense. The order also disqualifies firms for specified integrity, discrimination or wage theft violations while making the disclosures public.

Not With Our Money, the campaign that joined Johnson at the announcement, identified $3.19 billion in Chicago contractors held by 42 firms that also do business with ICE, according to the group's research.

Dhs Issues Scathing Rebuke After Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms Touts Cutting Ties With Ice

Johnson was referring to an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission proposal to rescind requirements for employers and other covered entities to file annual EEO reports containing aggregate employee race, sex and job-category data. EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas said the reports risked hindering enforcement of equal employment laws and raised constitutional concerns.

The order marks Johnson's latest clash with federal immigration authorities.

In October, Johnson barred ICE from using city parking lots and garages for operations, a policy a federal agent said forced agents to stage in public and created operational risks. DHS said Operation Midway Blitz had resulted in more than 4,500 arrests by December.

Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson's office for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

Original article

title: Trump still teases a third presidential run, but he's talking more and more about life after 2028
description: President Donald Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen — even as he's acknowled...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen — even as he's acknowledged the Constitution prohibits it.

But lately, Trump has begun showing signs that even he doesn't really believe another run will happen.

During recent speeches, the Republican president has begun describing life after the White House when his term ends in January 2029, predicting he'll be at home and agonizing as his successor claims credit for his accomplishments.

"Your next president is going to say, 'What a great job I did,'" Trump told an event on Long Island, New York, this month. "He'll be sitting around, watching television. A real stiff. Unless you vote Republican, of course."

A sitting president talking about becoming a former one is always politically fraught. But with midterm elections now just nine weeks away, Trump is approaching the point of his presidency where there will be more and more reminders that his power will soon wane.

Being willing to say he's contemplating a White House without him marks a notable shift for Trump. Going back to his first term and from virtually the moment he won a second, he's left the door open to staying put for more than eight years.

"He is all over the place," said Brian Kalt, a Michigan State University constitutional law professor. "And what that does is, it allows him to point to his own words to support any number of mutually exclusive things."

Trump can say, "'Oh yeah, I made it clear that I wasn't gonna run,'" Kalt said. "Or, if he decides that he will, he could say, 'Well, you know, I never said I wouldn't.'"

The White House dismissed suggestions that Trump's thoughts are increasingly turning to the clock running out on his presidency — and the legacy he'll leave behind. Spokesperson Olivia Wales said he "is fighting every day" to deliver on promises to reduce violent crime,crack down on the U. S-Mexico border and lower prescription drug prices.

"The only legacy President Trump is concerned with is making America greater than ever before," Wales said.

Still, hinting at how he'll be remembered is something Trump is suddenly talking about a lot.

During a recent Pennsylvania rally, he said, "Whoever the next president is, he's going to be talking about what a brilliant president he is. And I'll be home. And I'll be saying, 'That son of a gun,' because we did the job."

A week later in Georgia, Trump was predicting that once his presidency was over, "I'll be sitting home."

"I may be crying," the president added, arguing that Democrats could retake the Senate and scrap filibuster rules, making it easier to move their key legislation.

Then, in Michigan, Trump injected some doubt into whether he was ready to hand over the Oval Office and move back to Florida.

"In two and a half years, you may have a different president — may," he said, emphasizing the "may."

"I'll be sitting home. I'll be reading the papers. I'll be watching television," Trump said, before swiping at his predecessor, President Joe Biden. "And I'll be having some guy — like last time, a real idiot — stand up and say, 'We are doing record business.'"

But even as he's begun to suggest he'll be leaving the presidency, Trump has also continued to tease a 2028 reelection run.

Addressing the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association dinner last month, Trump joked, "Just like my presidency, the second time is always better" and that "the third time will be better yet. I'm only kidding." He later wore a 2028 campaign cap to finish the speech.

The Constitution's 22nd Amendment says no one can be elected president more than twice. It was ratified in 1951, six years after President Franklin Delano Roosevelt died, months into his fourth term. Until Roosevelt, no other president had defied the tradition of stepping down after two terms that George Washington started.

Still, Trump had only been back in the White House for a couple of months when he told NBC News, "There are methods which you could" use to seek a third term.

He acknowledged that one method was to be the running mate to Vice President JD Vance in 2028 — then have Vance step aside if the pair won.

"There are others, too," Trump said then, alluding to more options. He later told Time Magazine, "There are some loopholes," while also saying he didn't believe in using them.

The president has since often used his social media posts to promote "Trump 2028" logos featuring his slogan "Make America Great Again."

But Trump has also at times seemed definitive about the ban on him making another run, acknowledging recently to reporters: "I'd love to run, but the law is very strong."

Kalt wrote about a two-term president possibly getting back to office by running for vice president in "constitutional Cliffhangers: A Legal Guide for Presidents and Their Enemies."

"People do tend to find, in Trump's words, whatever it is that they want to hear," he said.

Second-term presidents typically see their power and influence wane during their last two years, particularly if their party suffers big midterm defeats. But Trump's comments could also be a sign he's thinking about cementing his legacy, a stage that many of his predecessors also reached.

"They all, particularly as they cross the midpoint of their second term, start thinking about legacy," said Paul Begala, a former adviser to President Bill Clinton.

"They all banish the word. I know Clinton and Bush, they said, 'Can't use the L-word.' But they do," Begala said, referring to his old boss Clinton and to President George W. Bush. "They all think about it. And the staff thinks about it and the Cabinet thinks about it."

In his last two years of office, Clinton threw himself into trying to broker a Middle East peace agreement. Bush used the slogan "sprint to the finish" during his presidency's final year in 2008, and Biden adopted a "run through the tape" ethos after abandoning his reelection bid.

Trump has leaned into molding the White House and Greater Washington in his own image, harkening back to his days as a real estate developer in 1970s and 1980s New York.

He's ordered up a towering arch near the Lincoln Memorial and restored city fountains, while constructing a Rose Garden patio area and helipad on the White House lawn and adding scores of gilded touches to the building's stately interior and exterior.

And then, there's the massive ballroom that Trump has crews rushing to finish in the face of legal challenges — a project the president says will only be completed late in 2028, shortly before he leaves office.

"It's not for me, 'cause I'm going to be here a very short period of time" when the work is finished, Trump recently told reporters in the Oval Office. "I'll be there for four, five, six months. This is for future presidents."

title: Iran’s president admits ‘we have many problems’ and missiles ‘are of no use’ as the U.S. chokes its economy while weakening Tehran’s grip on Hormuz
description: "People are on the edge now; if I put more pressure on them, they might fall off the edge. We have to be careful that no one falls off."
fullText:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged his country's economic woes amid pressure from the U.S., which is strangling its trade while protecting other countries' ships carrying oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Recent weeks have seen Tehran lose leverage over the critical energy chokepoint as traffic picks up, especially via a southern route along Oman's coast. At the same time, warnings about Iran's economy from Pezeshkian and the regime's other relative moderates have been mounting.

In an interview with state media on Friday, he signaled defiance in the face of all the economic pressure and credited Iran's resilience to its unity.

"We have many problems," Pezeshkian said, according to a Google translation. "There's inflation, economic issues, employment and many other problems, but the people are with us."

Indeed, inflation has soared above 80%, with prices for certain food staples up 100%. The International Monetary Fund said in April Iran's economy will shrink 6.1% this year, the worst contraction in decades. And a labor ministry official estimated that more than 1 million jobs had been lost by late May.

In an apparent dig at Iranian hardliners who reject negotiations with the U.S. and favor continued war, Pezeshkian added that "we may have many things; we may even have missiles and bombs, but they are of no use."

He later noted that imports are not coming into the country, including gasoline. The naval blockade has not only prevented Iran from exporting oil via its ports, it has also kept out imports of refined fuels that Iran needs despite being a major oil producer.

That has created shortages and long lines at gas stations, made worse by deep subsidies that encourage excess consumption. In the interview, Pezeshkian described efforts to curb fuel demand and hike prices, but hinted they can't go too far.

"We shouldn't make someone whose life revolves around gasoline suffer," he explained. "We shouldn't put more pressure on those who are already under pressure. People are on the edge now; if I put more pressure on them, they might fall off the edge. We have to be careful that no one falls off."

Pezeshkian estimated that Iranian trade has plunged 25%-35%, with imports down significantly more than exports. In fact, trade intelligence firm Kpler said Iran's August crude export loadings have collapsed more than 80% compared to a year ago.

Since the naval blockade was reimposed, U.S. force have redirected 82 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two to ensure compliance, Central Command said on Friday.

"Some people say that sanctions have no effect at all," Pezeshkian said. "I really don't know what to tell these people. I just want to say this, saying that sanctions have no effect is not consistent with these facts."

While the U.S. military tightens its chokehold, it is simultaneously loosening Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, Central Command said U.S. forces completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.

Estimates vary on exactly how much oil is leaking through, but the upshot is the volumes are substantial albeit still well short of normal. According to Goldman Sachs, total exports of crude and oil products from the region have risen to 15 million-16 million barrels a day. And Kpler said oil flows from the Persian Gulf have recovered to around 70% of pre-war levels.

U.S. officials told Axios that about 10 million barrels of oil a day are being transported out of the strait through the Omani corridor the U.S. military is defending.

A two-week stretch of U.S. bombing last month degraded Iran's radar and maritime surveillance systems, the report said, making it easier for tankers to sail through undetected at night with their transponders turned off. This has allowed vessels to make shuttle runs in and out, then unload oil to other tankers that deliver the cargo to customers.

To be sure, Iran is still attacking ships, but that hasn't been enough to stop traffic. Meanwhile, the U.S. military continues to weaken Iran's ability to close the strait. On Sunday, U.S. forces struck Iranian rocket launchers that were preparing to deploy sea mines in the strait.

Gregory Brew, an expert on Iran and oil at the Eurasia Group, said on X on Friday that Iran overplayed its hand in July, when it resumed attack on shipping in the strait's southern route.

"The result: the MOU is dead, the blockade is back in place, and the US is succeeding (to a partial, but notable extent) at reopening the strait without another deal," he added. "Perhaps the status quo swings back in Iran's favor, but right now this looks like a miscalculation to me."

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Trump says Iran's Kharg is being 'blown to smithereens', but gives no details
description: Iran's energy hub of Kharg Island is being blown to smithereens, U. President Donald Trump said on Sunday in a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Iran's energy hub of Kharg Island is being blown to smithereens, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday in a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video clip.

There was no other evidence that the Iranian energy hub was under attack. ‌The White House and the U.S. Defense Department did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours.

There was no immediate response to ‌Trump's post on Iranian media.

"Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT," Trump said on social media, but gave no further details.

Attacking Kharg, which handled 90% of Iran's oil exports before the war launched by U.S. and Israeli attacks on February 28, would severely disrupt its energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy.

Iran responded to an earlier U.S. attack on rocket launchers on its island of Larak, about 660 km (410 miles) east of Kharg, with an assault on two U.S. bases in Jordan, Iranian media said.

The return to hostilities followed weeks in which the Trump administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away ‌from military options.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday ⁠new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.

"We're starting with the banks, and we're telling the banks it's not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime," Bessent said in an interview.

After ⁠imposing penalties on the United Arab Emirates branches of Egypt's Banque Misr on Friday over alleged financial links to Iran, Bessent said the next step may be cutting off an institution entirely from the dollar-based financial system.

"You're going to see a lot more of these every week," Bessent told Reuters, ahead of a meeting of Group of 20 finance leaders.

FIRST KNOWN MILITARY ATTACKS IN WEEKS

In describing the ​first ​known U.S. military strikes since late July, a U.S. official said forces attacked two Iranian launchers on Larak ​Island.

The small island in the Strait of Hormuz near the strategic ‌port of Bandar Abbas overlooks shipping lanes at the mouth of the Gulf, giving it a key role in tension over Iran, maritime security and global energy supplies.

"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz," the source added.

In retaliation, Iran launched ballistic missiles at Jordan, targeting two U.S. bases. Jordan's armed forces had intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace, state television said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and vowed a "response and punishment" from Tehran, according to Iranian state media.

In a statement, the U.S. Central Command said it took "limited, precise" action against minelaying forces of Iran's Revolutionary Guards that posed an "imminent threat" in the Strait ‌of Hormuz. It gave no details.

After the U.S. strikes, Iran attacked U.S. forces station in Jordan, a ​Fox News reporter said on Sunday, citing a U.S. source. Nearly all incoming missiles "have been intercepted at this ​point," the reporter said on X, flagging a lack of significant impact.

Amid threats to ​shipping, the number of visible commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to five a day over the weekend, shipping data showed.

The actual ‌number could be higher as some vessels have switched off automatic identification ​systems to evade attacks.

Last week, U.S. President ​Donald Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait and Iran had been warned that any vessel placing new mines would be destroyed.

While Trump has repeatedly said the Strait of Hormuz is open, Iran's Revolutionary Guards' navy had called those statements "an obvious lie", reiterating that it remained closed ​to ships without Iranian permission.

The waterway carried nearly a fifth of ‌global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before it was blockaded in the six-month-old Iran war.

Iran is the third largest producer in the Organization ​of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.

title: Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns
description:
Exclusive: Patients identify errors in consultation transcripts that are missed by GPs, Healthwatch England finds
AI technology that listens to and transcribes patients’ consultations with doctors can put them at risk by getting the names of drugs and illnesses wrong, an NHS watchdog has warned.
In one case a woman was left badly shaken when the AI scribe’s summary of her conversation wrongly said she had demyelination – serious nerve damage that can lead to multiple sclerosis.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Exclusive: Patients identify errors in consultation transcripts that are missed by GPs, Healthwatch England finds

AI technology that listens to and transcribes patients’ consultations with doctors can put them at risk by getting the names of drugs and illnesses wrong, an NHS watchdog has warned.

In one case a woman was left badly shaken when the AI scribe’s summary of her conversation wrongly said she had demyelination – serious nerve damage that can lead to multiple sclerosis.

It was only when the patient, an NHS health professional, queried the AI tool’s record of the result of her MRI scan that the hospital corrected it to what it should have been – “null demyelination”.

“This was eventually corrected but was a very traumatising experience to be given an incorrect diagnosis because of AI and then be told it’s a typo,” said the woman, who asked not to be named.

Healthwatch England has highlighted the case and other mistakes by AI scribes to show that the technology, which the NHS is rolling out rapidly, is a potential threat to patient safety. Unless detected, errors could end up in patients’ medical records and affect their care, it said.

In another case, an AI scribe confused the drug the GP had prescribed with a different one of a similar name – a blunder which again the patient, rather than the doctor, identified. On another occasion an AI-generated summary letter did not say that the hospital consultant had told the patient to seek a repeat prescription from their GP for their migraine, which could have left them unable to get their medication.

Healthwatch, the statutory NHS patient champion, has heard “multiple stories from patients who have noticed these errors when a health professional hasn’t”, it said. “These inaccuracies may persist in their records if the patient doesn’t catch them.”

The government’s 10-year health plan for the NHS in England expects AI scribes to “liberate staff from their current burden of bureaucracy and administration, freeing up time to care and to focus on the patient”. It is central to the planned “big shift” for the NHS from being an analogue to a digital-based service.

A Healthwatch spokesperson said: “Healthcare has never been error-free. But our findings show the urgent need for clarity over how patients can report and get corrected any mistakes made by AI scribing tools or the professionals that use them.”

Rachel Power, chief executive of the Patients Association, said: “Trust and confidence in this technology depend on good communication and genuine partnership with patients and right now both are missing.”

Healthwatch added that it was “worrying” that the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has decided not to classify AI scribes as medical devices, which means there will be no England-wide oversight to ensure they are safe to use and effective.

GPs and hospital doctors in England are already using 27 different AI scribes.

Ministers have been warned that the NHS and medics could be sued over mistakes made by AI.

AI’s accuracy was in the spotlight recently when patients in Rotherham complained to their local Healthwatch that an AI receptionist used by some local GP practices did not understand their strong Yorkshire accents.

Dr Shier Ziser Dawood, a GP in London, last year warned in a leading medical journal that AI scribes may prove “a double-edged sword” for family doctors.

She recounted that an AI scribe said she had told her patient to “continue their Prozac” even though she had not prescribed or discussed that drug with them. That is an example of what are known as “hallucinations”, where AI scribes refer to something that was not raised during the consultation.

She warned that the need for doctors to review all transcripts in order to check for errors meant that AI tools are not yet proving time-saving.

Given the belief of NHS bosses that scribes will mean GPs no longer have to take notes during an appointment, family doctors may be expected to see two more patients every day, even though NHS GP consultation times are already some of the shortest in the world, Dawood added, writing in the British Journal of General Practice.

Dr Charlotte Blease, an expert in AI use in healthcare at Uppsala university in Sweden, said: “AI can and does make mistakes.”

Her research found that GPs who use ambient voice technology believe that errors are more likely to creep in when the consultation is with more than one person, with patients with a complex medical history, and with those whose first language is not English.

But, she added: “The fact is, doctors can and do make mistakes without AI. And it is certainly possible the error rate is worse.”

More than half the 1,003 UK GPs in her survey last year believed that their ambient AI records were more accurate than those produced themselves, Blease said.

title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026
description:
There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
• See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here
After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.
fullText:
After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.

 4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

Billed as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.

 10 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.

 15 September; PS5

The tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimed Fire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.

 17 September; Switch 2

Silent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …

 24 September; PC, PS5

Remedy Entertainment sets out to disprove the notion that all video game sequels are more of the same. This follow-up to the successful 2019 sci-fi shooter has a new lead character with supernatural powers, a whole new role-playing adventure feel, and a fresh take on Manhattan, where a reality-bending monster awaits …

 24 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The latest gorgeously strange game from Patapon creator Hiroyuki Kotani is a rhythm action platformer set in a colourful world where enemies are defeated with songs and players can work together to produce devastating melodies. Imagine Dead Cells merged with PaRappa the Rapper and you’re getting close.

 15 October; PC, PS, Switch, Xbox

The world-beating mega shooter packs its bags full of guns, grenades and macho dialogue and heads for Korea, in another Modern Warfare instalment. There will be epic battles, sanitised politically adjacent themes and rip-roaring online multiplayer – plus, moustached SAS figurehead Captain Price will be tagging along for the ride. Resistance is futile.

 23 October; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

After a decade in development and several delays, Rockstar’s entertainment behemoth returns, following loved-up criminals Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they take on every scumbag Vice City has to offer. Already looking vibrant, expansive and lascivious, this is Bonnie and Clyde for the digital generation.

 19 November; PS5, Xbox

title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20
description:
Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system
The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology.
In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system

The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology.

In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”.

He said the models risked destabilising the “highly interconnected” global financial system via cyber-disruption that “can spread across jurisdictions”.

Bailey wrote to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors before their meeting in North Carolina, US, this week: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release, and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond”.

His letter adds to alarm bells about AI that have been sounded by prominent technologists over the past few weeks – and mirrors his previous calls for international cooperation to tackle growing AI threats, when he told City bosses: “No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.”

Last month, a letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind – also shone a light on the concerns of the engineers working on the technology every day.

It stated: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” before going on to ask for the US government’s support for “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.

Earlier this month, it also emerged that OpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its cutting-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.

Extending this theme into the world of financial policy, Bailey continued: “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber-risk. Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber-risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers.”

Bailey called on those tasked with safeguarding the world’s financial systems to prioritise “appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis”.

The letter also noted Bailey’s concerns about the increased use of leverage in bond and equity markets, which he said was combining with high valuations in concentrated financial markets – particularly fuelled by investor optimism about the prospects of AI – in a way that could amplify a future market correction.

“I remain concerned therefore that a large shock or combination of shocks could concurrently trigger multiple vulnerabilities,” Bailey wrote.

Bailey has been governor of the Bank of England since March 2020, and previously headed both the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority, the UK’s two main financial regulators. He was appointed chair of the FSB last year.

The FSB, based in Basel, Switzerland, coordinates the work at international level of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies in an effort to develop effective regulation and policies in the interest of financial stability.

title: Swansea agree loan of Man City's Monga as Walta to leave
description: Manchester City winger Jeremy Monga is set for a season at Swansea City, who will allow Finland international Leo Walta to join Los Angeles on loan.
fullText:
Swansea City are poised to complete the loan signing of Manchester City's Jeremy Monga and will let Leo Walta leave the club on loan.

A deal has been agreed to recruit 17-year-old winger Monga, who is due to travel to Swansea to undergo a medical with a view to completing a season-long loan switch prior to Tuesday's 23:00 BST transfer deadline.

Finland international Walta was omitted from the matchday squad for Swansea's 3-0 win at Derby County on Saturday and is set to join Major League Soccer side Los Angeles.

It comes as Championship side Swansea are also closing in on the signing of Huddersfield Town midfielder Tom Iorpenda.

Swans close in on Huddersfield midfielder Iorpenda

Swansea can still improve after unbeaten start - Matos

Monga is a product of Leicester City's academy and made his senior debut for the Foxes as a 15-year-old during the 2024-25 campaign.

He featured 30 times for Leicester in the Championship last season before signing a five-year deal with Man City earlier this summer.

During his time at Leicester, Monga became the youngest goal scorer in the Championship when he netted in his side's 2-1 defeat by Preston North End in August last year.

Upon completing the signing of Monga earlier this summer, City director of football Hugo Viana hailed the teenager as an "exciting player" and added he has "already made huge strides in his young career".

The England Under-19 international is now set to spend the remainder of the current campaign on loan with Vitor Matos' side.

The Swans have already bolstered their wide options with the additions of Elijah Just, Moussa Yeo and Joseph Opoku this summer.

Walta joined on an initial loan deal from Swedish outfit Sirius in February - a switch that was made permanent by the Swans earlier this summer.

His sole league appearance this season came as a late substitute in Swansea's opening day 2-1 win at Stoke City - although he also came off the bench in his side's 1-0 EFL Cup first round loss to Birmingham City.

The 23-year-old made 10 league appearances for Swansea in the latter stages of the 2025-26 season and scored his only goal for the club in a 3-1 victory over Charlton Athletic on the final day of the campaign.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds

Swansea's midfield department has undergone numerous changes over recent months.

The Swans sold Ethan Galbraith to Championship rivals Stoke City earlier this summer and are also without Goncalo Franco until October after the Portuguese midfielder underwent ankle surgery.

Matos has already bolstered his options in the centre of the park by recruiting Canada international Stephen Eustaquio from Porto.

That deal came after Swansea signed New Zealand international Just - who can play out wide or centrally - from Scottish outfit Motherwell.

They also have Jay Fulton, Melker Widell and Marko Stamenic in midfield while summer signing Moussa Yeo, who is predominantly a winger, can operate as an attacking midfielder.

Swansea - who remain unbeaten in the league this season - return to Championship action against Watford at the Swansea.com Stadium on Tuesday night (19:45 BST).

title: Taylor v Pili - all you need to know
description: All you need to know about Katie Taylor's farewell fight against Flora Pili at Croke Park in Dublin on Saturday night.
fullText:
After almost a decade as a professional boxer, Katie Taylor will call time on her career after her 27th and final bout on Saturday.

The Irish superstar, 40, will aim to become a three-time undisputed world champion against Frenchwoman Flora Pili in Dublin.

Taylor, who has won 25 professional fights and avenged her only defeat against Chantelle Cameron, will defend her light-welterweight WBO, WBA and IBF titles against Pili, who boasts an unbeaten 12-0 record.

With the vacant WBC title on the line, the Bray fighter has finally got her dream bout at Croke Park as 80,000 fans are expected to pack out the stadium.

Will Taylor claim a fairytale farewell on home soil? Or will 29-year-old Pili spoil the party and pull off a huge upset?

Here is all you need to know about Taylor v Pili.

Live text commentary will begin at 20:00 BST on the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also follow the action through fight week on BBC Sport via the 5 Live Boxing podcast.

Taylor and Pili are scheduled to make their ringwalks at about 22:10.

All timings are estimated and subject to change.

Katie Taylor v Flora Pili - WBA, WBO, WBC & IBF light-welterweight world titles

Paddy Donovan v Tyrone McKenna - welterweight

Taylor Bevan v Emmet Brennan - super-middleweight

Joe McGrail v Matthew Boreland - super-bantamweight

Dave Allen v Thomas Cartey - heavyweight

Molly McCann v Sylwia Doligala - bantamweight

Following a decorated amateur career, which included winning gold at the 2012 Olympics, Taylor quickly established herself as a dominant force once turning professional in 2016.

Taylor claimed three stoppage wins in her first five professional bouts and landed her first world title in her seventh contest, claiming the vacant WBA lightweight belt, with a unanimous decision victory over Anahi Ester Sanchez in Cardiff.

The rest of Taylor's career has played out at the very highest level, competing across 20 successive world title bouts and winning 19 of them.

Defeat by Cameron, which Taylor avenged in their rematch, remains the only loss on her 26-fight record. Taylor has six victories via knockout.

Pili, 11 years younger than Taylor, has won all 12 of her fights as a professional - winning two by knockout.

Just two of her fights have taken place outside her native France, earning victories in Italy and Luxembourg.

There could hardly be a more fitting setting for Taylor's final fight. She has wanted to headline at Croke Park for years - and it promises to be a celebration of one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures.

Reports suggest many in attendance will be experiencing a live boxing event for the first time, underlining the extent of Taylor's influence beyond the sport.

When Taylor was growing up, females were not permitted to box in Ireland. She went on to become a trailblazer for the sport, winning Olympic gold at London 2012 and inspiring a generation of female fighters.

Her professional career has been equally remarkable. She has consistently broken new ground on the biggest stages.

Her trilogy with Amanda Serrano produced three landmark encounters, beginning with their first meeting at a sold-out Madison Square Garden in 2022. Their subsequent rematches were broadcast globally on Netflix, expanding the reach of women's boxing even further.

Taylor is already a two-weight undisputed world champion and aims to secure undisputed status for a third time in her farewell bout.

Mandatory challenger Pili has earned her opportunity and cannot be overlooked, but Taylor remains the consummate professional and will be determined to conclude her career on a high.

title: Losing Gloucester captaincy was 'brutal' - Ludlow
description: Gloucester's Lewis Ludlow on losing the captaincy last season, his two England caps, and chasing a record in his upcoming testimonial season.
fullText:
Gloucester flanker Lewis Ludlow says it was "brutal" to lose the club captaincy last August and he would "take it back tomorrow" if offered.

Ludlow has played more than 250 games for the Cherry and Whites and his time as skipper between 2020 and 2025 makes him the longest-serving captain in the club's history.

However, the 31-year-old was replaced by Tomos Williams in the role for the 2025-26 season, although the Welshman signed for Saracens this summer.

"It was brutal," Ludlow told BBC Radio Gloucestershire about being told he was no longer captain.

"I didn't change personally, but it takes some getting used to."

Singleton nearing end of rehab but leaves Gloucester

Gloucester decide against Villa Park return

Champions Saints host Newcastle on opening weekend

Ludlow was speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire for an hour-long interview special as he prepares for his testimonial season at the Prem club.

While he felt the captaincy change was coming, he was still surprised when the conversation happened during pre-season.

"I'd kind of prepared myself for it because it was always going to happen at some point," he said.

"I didn't think it would be that timing but it was and I felt like the only thing I could do then was worry about my rugby and be the best bloke I could be to help Tommy [Williams].

"From what people have said, I did that. I'm probably prouder of that than anything. I've been in changing rooms where people aren't that bloke and it makes it very difficult. But I didn't want that to be the case."

Despite the change Ludlow said team-mates still often referred to him as 'Skip' and referees would seek him out post-match as they were so used to him being captain.

However, he believes he and Williams created a working relationship that still allowed Ludlow to use his authority in the team.

"We did as good as we could in terms of balancing him being captain, me still leading where I could and trying to be as effective as possible," Ludlow said.

Ludlow has also worn the captain's armband for England, although remarkably the two games in which he captained his country in 2021 remain the only two he has ever played at international level.

He was named captain by then head coach Eddie Jones for matches against the USA and Canada at a time when an array of players were away on Lions duty and Jones was looking to widen his squad before the 2023 World Cup.

Ludlow became just the fifth player to ever captain England on his debut.

But after receiving a red card against Canada, and a subsequent four-game ban for foul play, he never played for England again even though Jones wrote a letter of praise for his disciplinary committee.

"It was possibly the nicest thing anyone's ever written about me and he [Jones] explained why he picked me as captain, the leadership skills I've shown and how he'd been to watch all the games during the season," Ludlow said.

"It was what I was doing in the warm-ups, what I was doing in the huddles, what I was doing post-game, which is why he wanted to make me the captain."

Ludlow was called into training camps in the period that followed but said he has no regrets about never pulling on a Red Rose shirt again.

"When I finished that summer I'd never been fitter, I'd never been stronger," he said.

"We played some class rugby in those two games and I got to become the fifth person to captain my country ever on debut and for that I'll always be grateful."

The 2026-27 season will be Ludlow's 14th at Gloucester after coming through their academy and he has his sights on surpassing Nick Wood's all-time club record of 277 appearances in the professional era.

Ludlow said his body feels "really good" going into the new season after his 2025-26 campaign was disrupted by persistent injuries to his hand and wrist that meant undergoing surgery in April.

The surgery, which fused joints in his thumb on his right hand, means he finally feels pain free for the first time in five years, even though he will continue to wear a cast during games.

Because of the pain he sometimes could not pick up his young son, or even pick up everyday items like a kettle or saucepan.

"To be able to just do normal everyday tasks without things hurting as much as they did, it's quite strange really, but it was a nice feeling," he said.

Ludlow has two clear goals for his testimonial season, which has events scheduled over the next 12 months.

The first is to raise money for two charities: 4Ed, which was set up by his friend and former team-mate Ed Slater after he was diagnosed with motor neurone disease, and the National Foundation for Retired Service Animals. The second is to break Wood's record.

"I want to give as much to those two charities as possible to be able to make a statement of 'this is what I've given these guys' and be able to list off to fans where it's gone and how it's done and how it's worked out," he said.

"And then during the season I need 13 games. It'd be an amazing testimonial season to break Woody's record.

"I know when and where it should be, but there's a long way to go before then."

title: Ali 'The Greatest' but Maguire the latest to win in Croke Park
description: With Katie Taylor set to be the first boxer to headline Croke Park since Muhammad Ali beat Al 'Blue' Lewis in 1972, BBC Sport NI catches up with Paddy Maguire, who was last to box on that iconic night.
fullText:
Croke Park's storied history contains some of Irish sport's most seminal moments.

Primarily a stadium for Gaelic games, there have been occasions when other sports graced the hallowed turf and on 19 July 1972, punches replaced points as Muhammad Ali took on Al 'Blue' Lewis.

When Katie Taylor makes her final career ringwalk on Saturday with the undisputed light-welterweight crown on offer against Flora Pili, 54 years will have passed since 'The Greatest' starred at the since redeveloped venue.

While Ali was the main attraction in 1972, it was Belfast's Paddy Maguire who boxed last on that balmy Wednesday evening, coming through on points against France's Guy Caudron.

"It's hard to believe it has taken so long for boxing to return to Croke Park," Maguire told BBC Sport NI.

As an amateur, Maguire won featherweight silver at the 1966 Commonwealth Games in Jamaica - a medal that was "hard won as they were all tough fights".

A switch to the professional code prompted another move, this time to London where he linked up with manager Paddy Byrne.

It was this relationship which ultimately led to Maguire and Pat McCormack earning a slot on Ali's undercard, which also featured Donegal's Paddy Doherty, plus future light-heavyweight world champion John Conteh and heavyweight Joe Bugner, who would twice lose to Ali in later years.

"Pat and myself were great friends and had the same manager, so it was great for us to be on such a huge bill," Maguire recalled.

"To be a man from the Kashmir Road in Belfast, fighting on Muhammad Ali's bill was great, but I could never understand why there were so few Irish fighters involved."

Aged 30, Ali - who had iconic wins against George Foreman and Joe Frazier to come in his career - accepted a reported £300,000 offer by Kerry promoter Michael 'Butty' Sugrue to fight in Ireland.

Battling a cold, Ali secured an 11th-round victory over Lewis and while just 17,000 made their way through the turnstiles - 15,000 short of the break-even mark -others were more creative in how they entered.

One of those attending by conventional means was Kilkenny hurling great Eddie Keher in a year in which he collected the fourth of his six All-Ireland senior medals.

A boxing fan, Keher recalls burning the midnight oil in his youth with his father, tuning into radio commentary of heavyweight greats Joe Louis, Rocky Marciano and then Ali.

With the promotional push for Croke Park in full swing, an idea was hatched to have the pair meet at the Kilternan Hotel - "a high point" in his life.

"I was dumbstruck when I saw him [Ali]. He was different from what I imagined because he wasn't the flamboyant guy we'd seen on television," Keher told BBC Sport NI's GAA Social podcast.

"The press were outside and I had two hurls and a sliotar [ball]. I was supposed to teach him how to play hurling, but he was finding it hard to hit the ball with two hands, so he was hitting it with one hand like a tennis racquet.

"He was still the ordinary guy but then he came up close to me and said, 'we'll put on a show for these guys' so he went to hit me with his hurl and I put up mine to save me. Then he was going around fencing with the hurl and became the Muhammad Ali we knew."

While Keher and those in attendance remember the occasion with fondness, behind the scenes things were a little more chaotic.

Fight gloves had not been sourced, prompting a last-minute scramble to have some sent from England, resulting in a late start to the undercard which would ultimately leave Maguire waiting until after the main event before he boxed.

"There weren't too many left by that stage, but I ended up on last as I was seen as an exciting, all-action pressure fighter," Maguire reasoned.

"Maybe their idea was to have me on last to try and keep people there."

Maguire remembers Ali as a "lovely man" - and it would not be the last time the boxers' paths would cross.

After British and Commonwealth bantamweight title defeats, Maguire would avenge a previous loss against David Needham in 1975 to get his hands on the Lonsdale Belt - and in the build-up, reunited with Ali at Wembley.

In August 1977, they met again in the Grosvenor House Hotel for a testimonial in honour of Ali's friend Paddy Monaghan, the Fermanagh-born bare-knuckle boxer.

"There were ups and down," Maguire says of his career, "but it's one I'm proud of."

While his days in the ring were over, he would remain connected to the sport, serving as a member of the British Boxing Board of Control's Northern Ireland Council.

On Saturday, Maguire will watch from home as Taylor, a trailblazer for women's boxing, makes the same walk as Ali.

"I've had the opportunity to tell my kids and grandchildren about my time there, so for those boxing this time, they can do the same one day," he said.

"Katie Taylor has had a great career and deserves her big night, but hopefully it's not another 50 years before boxing's back in Croke Park."

title: Man Utd near deal for Mexico's Bernal
description: Manchester United are close to signing Mexico international Rebeca Bernal from Washington Spirit.
fullText:
Manchester United are close to signing Mexico international Rebeca Bernal from Washington Spirit.

The 29-year-old, who can play in the centre of either defence or midfield, would become the first Mexican to feature in the Women's Super League.

Bernal joined the Spirit in February 2025 from CF Monterrey and has played 41 times for them.

During her time in Washington, she won the NWSL Challenge Cup in 2025.

Bernal missed Spirit's NWSL game on Sunday against Bay FC with what the club described as an "excused absence".

She has also made 65 appearances for Mexico, scoring seven goals, including the winner in the 2023 Pan American Games women's football final as they beat Chile to claim the title for the first time.

United, who will start their WSL campaign under new manager Eva Olid at London City Lionesses on Friday, have signed defender Andrea Medina from Atletico Madrid, goalkeeper Janina Leitzig from Leicester City and Sweden winger Monica Jusu Bah from BK Hacken.

title: British tight end Traore makes Dolphins roster cut
description: British tight end Seydou Traore is included in the Miami Dolphins' initial 53-man roster, meaning he can play from the start of the 2026 NFL season.
fullText:
British tight end Seydou Traore has been included in the Miami Dolphins' initial 53-man roster, meaning he can play from the start of the 2026 NFL season.

The 24-year-old was drafted by the Dolphins in the fifth round of the 2026 NFL Draft in April, becoming the first graduate of England's NFL Academy to complete his pathway to the NFL.

However, despite signing a four-year rookie contract worth $4.8m (£3.6m), he still needed to survive the roster cut from 90 or 91 players to 53.

Traore was born in France but raised in London, where he played for the London Warriors before joining the NFL Academy in 2019.

The academy was set up to help international players earn college scholarships and prepare them for the NFL.

Traore joined Clearwater Academy in Florida before enrolling at Arkansas State University in 2021. He transferred to Mississippi State University in 2023 before entering the draft earlier this year.

His selection in the draft was announced by former NFL defensive end Efe Obada, who also began his journey into American football with the London Warriors.

Meanwhile, Northern Irish kicker Charlie Smyth has been released by the New Orleans Saints after making his NFL debut last season.

title: From playing Serena Williams on screen to US Open
description: Having played a young Serena Williams on the big screen, teenager Thea Frodin is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.
fullText:
Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.

Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'.

That involved the then 12-year-old working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus.

"Being able to play the role of somebody that I looked up to for my whole life was super special," Frodin told the WTA website., external

"I was honoured. She was one of the players that I looked up to most, just when I was starting to play.

"She's such an inspiration to me."

Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles.

To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion.

"I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin.

"This is a huge opportunity for me to enjoy the moment, have fun and see what I can do.

"The atmosphere, how loud the crowd will be, I feel like I fit well in that environment."

Venus Williams loses 15th match in row in 2am finish

Frodin, who is ranked 580th in the world, worked on set with Hollywood star Smith for a few days a week over a period of six months.

She has fond memories of her experience working with Oscar-winner Smith, who would always remember to bring hot water to shoots to keep Frodin warm during their cold, rainy days filming out on the courts.

During that time, she became so accustomed to playing like 23-time major singles champion Serena that her coaches had to help her rediscover her natural style.

"After I was done shooting, I got used to her strokes," Frodin told the US Open website.

"My coaches were a bit frustrated because I naturally started to hit like her.

"I picked up Serena's backhand, but I tried as much as possible to go back to my strokes."

Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit

It has not taken long for Frodin to secure her maiden appearance at the sport's highest level.

The 17-year-old earned a wildcard into this year's US Open women's singles competition - just as Venus Williams has done - by winning the United States Tennis Association' (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championships.

It comes in a year where Frodin reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open girls' singles - her best result as a junior at a major.

She also made her qualifying debut on the WTA Tour as a wildcard in Miami, and pushed former world number 35 Viktorija Golubic in a three-set loss in her first meeting with a player ranked inside the top-100.

But on Tuesday, she will walk out for the biggest match of her life.

"To be standing here right now and actually getting a chance to play in the main draw, it means everything," said Frodin.

"[Rybakina] is number two for a reason, so I'm expecting a battle. Hopefully, I can bring out my best level against her."

And, while she has never met the Williams sisters, Frodin is hoping that can change this fortnight.

"Hopefully, if I get a chance to hit with them or just meet them, anything, I'll take it," Frodin added.

"That would be incredible. That would be a dream."

title: Monza memories - Italian GP in pictures through the years
description: A selection of images from the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, which has hosted more Formula 1 races than any other circuit.
fullText:
The Italian Grand Prix takes place this weekend at Monza, arguably the most historic venue on the calendar.

Monza has hosted Formula 1 races more times than any other circuit, staging grands prix in all but one year since the inaugural season in 1950.

The only time Monza was absent was 1980, when it was being renovated.

Located in a royal park and surrounded by woodland, it is known as the 'cathedral of speed'. It is the spiritual home of Ferrari and the devoted tifosi who adore the Italian team.

It is all but impossible to imagine F1 without Monza - it was where the first world championship was decided 76 years ago and where, last year, Red Bull's Max Verstappen set the fastest lap in F1 history during qualifying.

Throughout the years, Monza has been the scene of thrilling finishes, Ferrari glory, title wins, controversy and tragedy. Its story is F1's story.
